content: 1. There is no new evidence that would alter the quality of the evidence or the strength of the recommendations provided. 2. The 2006 guidance introduced a symptom-based screening approach for evaluating child tuberculosis (TB) contacts. This approach has since been adopted for implementing isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT) in settings with high HIV prevalence and has been evaluated in that context. However, no prospective studies in children have been published to date. 3. The panel decided not to make changes to the recommendations but revised the wording to be more specific for children in the context of this guidance. 4. The recommended dosage of isoniazid for children, including for IPT, is 10 mg/kg per day, with a range of 7–15 mg/kg and a maximum dose of 300 mg/day. 5. Recommendation 18: Clinical evaluation of household and close contacts for active TB should be based on the risk of having or developing active TB or the potential consequences of the disease if it develops. Priority should be given to: Children with symptoms suggestive of TB, Children under 5 years of age, Children with known or suspected immunocompromising conditions (especially those living with HIV), and Child contacts of index cases with multidrug-resistant (MDR-TB) or extensively drug-resistant TB (XDR-TB) (proven or suspected). (Strong recommendation, very low quality of evidence). 6. Recommendation 19: Contact investigation is recommended for household and close contacts when the index case has any of the following characteristics: Sputum smear-positive pulmonary TB, MDR-TB or XDR-TB (proven or suspected), Is a person living with HIV (PLHIV), Is a child under 5 years of age. (Strong recommendation, very low quality of evidence). 7. Recommendation 20: Contact investigation may be conducted for household and close contacts of all other index cases with pulmonary TB, in addition to those covered in Recommendation 19. (Conditional recommendation, very low quality of evidence). 8. Recommendation 21: Children under 5 years of age who are household or close contacts of people with TB and who, after appropriate clinical evaluation, are found not to have active TB should be given 6 months of IPT (10 mg/kg per day, range 7–15 mg/kg, maximum dose 300 mg/day). (Strong recommendation, high quality of evidence). 9. Recommendation 22: In settings with high HIV prevalence, all household and close contacts of people with TB should be counseled and tested for HIV. (Strong recommendation, very low quality of evidence). 10. Recommendation 23: In settings with low HIV prevalence, all household and close contacts of people with TB who have symptoms compatible with active TB may be offered counseling and testing for HIV as part of their clinical evaluation. (Conditional recommendation, very low quality of evidence). 11. Recommendation 24: All household contacts of an index case who is a PLHIV should be counseled and tested for HIV. (Strong recommendation, very low quality of evidence). 12. The recommendations related to infection control do not specifically mention children but are relevant to all TB patients. The panel noted that these recommendations are related to strengthening health services and implementing activities at various levels of the health system. The principles of infection control outlined in the document are applicable to children. 13. The panel recognized that certain facility-based settings, such as neonatal care settings, pose a very high risk for children. However, no recommendations specific to children were made. 14. For children living with HIV, the panel reviewed evidence on isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT). While some studies showed benefits, others did not, and the evidence was conflicting. The panel noted that the epidemiological context of some studies may not be widely representative, and some studies predated the introduction of antiretroviral therapy (ART) in children. 15. In settings with high TB prevalence, 6 months of IPT may provide additional benefits to ART in protecting against TB. In settings with medium to low TB prevalence, IPT might be offered considering resource implications. The panel recommended further research in this area. 16. Recommendation 25: Children living with HIV who are more than 12 months of age and who are unlikely to have TB disease based on symptom-based screening and have no contact with a TB case: Should be offered 6 months of IPT (10 mg/kg per day, range 7–15 mg/kg, maximum dose 300 mg/day) as part of a comprehensive package of HIV prevention and care services if living in settings with high TB prevalence. (Strong recommendation, low quality of evidence). Might be offered 6 months of IPT (10 mg/kg per day, range 7–15 mg/kg, maximum dose 300 mg/day) as part of a comprehensive package of HIV prevention and care services if living in settings with medium or low TB prevalence. (Conditional recommendation acknowledging resource implications, low quality of evidence). 17. The panel recognized that ART improves treatment outcomes for TB in HIV-positive children. 18. Recommendation 27: Children with proven or suspected pulmonary TB or tuberculous meningitis caused by multidrug-resistant bacilli can be treated with a fluoroquinolone in the context of a well-functioning MDR-TB control program and within an appropriate MDR-TB regimen. The decision to treat should be made by a clinician experienced in managing pediatric TB. (Strong recommendation, very low quality of evidence). 19. The panel noted that treatment outcomes for MDR-TB in children are at least as good as those in adults and that treatment for drug-resistant TB in children is tolerated at least as well as in adults. However, no additional recommendations specific to children were made. 20. Recommendation 28: All children treated for TB should be recorded and reported by national tuberculosis programs (NTP) in one of two age bands (0–4 years and 5–14 years). (No change to recommendation, as it is derived from good clinical and public health practice). 21. Presumptive TB refers to a patient presenting with symptoms or signs suggestive of TB. TB cases are classified based on anatomical site of disease, history of previous treatment, drug resistance, and HIV status. 22. A bacteriologically confirmed TB case is one where a biological specimen is positive by smear microscopy, culture, or WHO-approved rapid diagnostics (e.g., Xpert MTB/RIF). All such cases should be notified, regardless of whether TB treatment has started. 23. A clinically diagnosed TB case is one that does not meet the criteria for bacteriological confirmation but has been diagnosed with active TB by a clinician and is being given a full course of TB treatment. This includes cases diagnosed based on X-ray abnormalities, suggestive histology, or extrapulmonary cases without laboratory confirmation. 24. Pulmonary TB (PTB) refers to any bacteriologically confirmed or clinically diagnosed case involving the lung parenchyma or tracheobronchial tree. Miliary TB is classified as PTB due to lung lesions. 25. Extrapulmonary TB refers to TB involving organs other than the lungs, such as the pleura, lymph nodes, abdomen, genitourinary tract, skin, joints, bones, or meninges. 26. Patients with both pulmonary and extrapulmonary TB should be classified as PTB. 27. TB cases are also classified based on history of previous treatment, focusing on whether the patient is new, has relapsed, or has been treated after failure or loss to follow-up. 28. HIV-positive TB patients are those with a positive HIV test result at the time of TB diagnosis or documented evidence of HIV care enrollment. HIV-negative TB patients are those with a negative HIV test result at the time of TB diagnosis.
